title: WHAT IF YOU DIE BELIEVING THE WRONG DOCTRINE—BUT YOU BELONG TO THE RIGHT SAVIOR?
paragraphs: WHAT IF YOU DIE BELIEVING THE WRONG DOCTRINE—BUT YOU BELONG TO THE RIGHT SAVIOR?
Can a Christian Be Truly Saved While Being Wrong About Secondary Doctrines? The Biblical Answer May Humble the Confident, Comfort the Confused, and Change How You See the Family of God.
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ.
Your earthly life is over. Every sermon you heard, every Bible study you attended, every theological argument you won, every doctrine you defended, and every mistake you made is now behind you.
And suddenly, the question that once seemed so important begins to sound very different.
What if you were wrong about something you sincerely believed the Bible taught?
What if the Christian you criticized for holding a different interpretation actually loved Jesus more deeply than you did?
What if the believer you dismissed as spiritually immature had spent years quietly feeding the hungry, forgiving enemies, praying through suffering, and clinging to Christ when nobody was watching?
And what if, despite all your theological knowledge, you had forgotten how to love the very people Jesus purchased with His blood?
There is something terrifying about being confidently wrong.
But there is something even more beautiful about a Savior whose power to save is greater than His children's ability to understand everything perfectly.
Here is the question that could change the way you see salvation forever:
Does Jesus save people because their theology is flawless, or does He save sinners who genuinely trust in Him, even while their understanding remains imperfect?
Before answering, we must be careful.
Because one careless answer could make biblical truth seem optional.
And another could make salvation seem impossible for anyone who has not mastered every disputed doctrine in Christianity.
Neither answer does justice to the Gospel.
And somewhere between arrogant certainty and careless compromise, Scripture gives us something far more glorious.
Grace that never abandons truth.
Truth that never makes grace unnecessary.
And a Savior who does not need imperfect people to become omniscient before He can redeem them.
THE MAN DYING BESIDE JESUS DID NOT HAVE TIME TO BECOME A THEOLOGIAN.
Picture Calvary.
Three crosses.
A dying criminal.
A bleeding Savior.
No comfortable church building. No theological library. No opportunity to attend years of discipleship classes.
Only a man confronting the wreckage of his life while death approached.
Luke 23:40–43 records something extraordinary.
One criminal rebuked the other, acknowledged that they were receiving the consequences of their crimes, and confessed that Jesus had done nothing wrong.
Then he turned toward Christ.
“Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, ESV)
And Jesus answered:
“Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, ESV)
Read that again.
Jesus did not say, “First, explain your position on the millennium.”
He did not demand that the man settle every disputed question concerning church government, spiritual gifts, or the precise sequence of future events.
He did not require a theological examination before extending mercy.
The dying criminal recognized his guilt, acknowledged Jesus' innocence and kingship, and appealed to Him for mercy.
And Jesus promised him paradise.
Now, we must not twist this passage.

The thief's experience does not prove that baptism, discipleship, obedience, and sound doctrine are unimportant. Jesus commanded His disciples to baptize and teach believers to obey everything He commanded (Matthew 28:19–20).
The extraordinary circumstances of a dying criminal do not cancel the ordinary responsibilities of Christian discipleship.
But they reveal something breathtaking about salvation.
The criminal was not saved by possessing complete theological knowledge. He was saved by the mercy of the King in whom he placed his hope.
And perhaps that should make every one of us a little slower to pronounce judgment on the eternal destiny of a fellow believer over a disputed secondary doctrine.
Because the Savior who welcomed that dying criminal is the same Savior who receives repentant sinners today.
But does that mean doctrine does not matter?
Absolutely not.
And this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
NOT EVERY THEOLOGICAL ERROR IS A SECONDARY ISSUE.
There is a difference between misunderstanding a biblical teaching and rejecting the Gospel itself.
The apostle Paul did not treat every doctrinal disagreement as equally serious.
In Galatians 1:8–9, he pronounced a severe warning against proclaiming a gospel contrary to the one the apostles had preached.
In 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, Paul summarized matters of first importance: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day.
These are not optional decorations around Christianity.
They concern the very foundation of the Christian faith.
Jesus Christ is not merely a moral teacher who offered helpful religious advice.
He is the eternal Son of God who became flesh (John 1:1, 14).
He died for sinners.
He rose bodily from the dead.
He is Lord.
And salvation comes through Him, not through our ability to earn God's acceptance.
Paul writes:
The original Greek makes this especially meaningful.
The expression χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι — chariti este sesōsmenoi means, in context, “by grace you have been saved.”
The construction emphasizes salvation as a reality brought about by God's gracious action, with continuing significance for those who have been saved.
The word χάρις — charis means grace, favor, or gift-like generosity.
And the verb behind σεσῳσμένοι — sesōsmenoi comes from σῴζω — sōzō, meaning to save, rescue, or deliver.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, “By flawless theological precision you have been saved.”
He does not say, “By winning every doctrinal debate you have been saved.”
He says salvation is by grace through faith.
But that faith is not faith in faith itself.
It is faith in Jesus Christ.
The object of saving faith matters.
The identity of the Savior matters.
The Gospel matters.
A person cannot simply redefine Jesus, reject His saving work, and assume that every religious belief leads to the same salvation.
Scripture does not permit that conclusion.
Yet Scripture also never teaches that a believer must achieve perfect understanding of every biblical subject before Christ can save them.
That distinction changes everything.
YOU CAN BE WRONG ABOUT SOMETHING IMPORTANT WITHOUT BEING WRONG ABOUT THE ONE WHO SAVES YOU.
Consider two sincere Christians.
One believes that Christ will return before a future thousand-year reign described in Revelation 20.
Another understands that passage differently.
Both confess that Jesus Christ will return, judge the living and the dead, defeat evil, and bring God's redemptive purposes to completion.
Their disagreement is meaningful.
They should study Scripture carefully.
They should not pretend the difference is imaginary.
But must one automatically be unsaved because their interpretation of the millennium is mistaken?
Scripture gives us no warrant to make that declaration.
Or consider believers who disagree about whether certain miraculous spiritual gifts continue in the church today.
One is a continuationist.
Another is a cessationist.
Both may genuinely confess Christ, trust His saving work, submit to Scripture, and seek to live holy lives.
Their interpretations cannot both be correct in every respect.
But theological disagreement does not automatically prove that one has never belonged to Jesus.
The same principle can apply to certain disagreements about worship practices, church governance, the timing of end-times events, and other disputed questions.
However, we must be precise.
Christians do not universally agree on which doctrines should be classified as secondary.

For example, baptism is commanded by Christ, and Christians disagree not only about its mode and subjects but also about its relationship to salvation. Those disagreements can have serious implications for church membership and fellowship.
Calling a doctrine secondary does not mean it is insignificant.
It means that an error concerning that doctrine does not necessarily amount to a denial of the saving Gospel.
That is an important distinction.
Because there is a dangerous difference between saying, “This doctrine matters,” and saying, “Anyone who disagrees with me about it is going to hell.”
One statement can express biblical conviction.
The other may claim authority over another person's eternal destiny that God has not given us.
PAUL ALREADY CONFRONTED THIS PROBLEM INSIDE THE EARLY CHURCH.
Imagine a Christian community divided over food.
Some believers were convinced that certain foods could be eaten freely.
Others abstained because of conscience.
To modern ears, that may sound insignificant.
But in the early church, these questions could touch religious identity, holiness, fellowship, and deeply held convictions.
The disagreement was real.
And Paul did not respond by pretending that truth was unknowable.
He addressed the issue while commanding believers to stop despising and condemning one another.
Romans 14:3 says:
“Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.” (ESV)
Then comes a question that should silence much of our spiritual arrogance.
“Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another?” (Romans 14:4, ESV)
Think about that.
A servant belongs to his master.
And a Christian belongs to Christ.
Paul was not saying that Christians should never evaluate teaching or confront sin.
Elsewhere, he explicitly commanded believers to guard sound doctrine and correct serious error.
He was addressing disputes in which believers were tempted to treat their own conscience and convictions as grounds for rejecting those whom God had received.
And Romans 14:17 gives us the wider perspective:
“For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.” (ESV)
That does not make biblical obedience irrelevant.
It reminds us that the kingdom is larger than the particular controversy consuming our attention.
Some Christians are so busy defending the boundaries of their theological position that they forget the Lord of the kingdom.
They can identify another person's doctrinal mistakes in seconds.
But they struggle to recognize pride in their own hearts.
They can explain the Greek tense of a verb.
But they cannot apologize to their spouse.
They can defend the doctrine of grace.
But they refuse to extend grace to a brother or sister.
And the tragedy is not that they care too much about truth.
The tragedy is that they have separated their defense of truth from the character of the Christ who is Truth.
KNOWING MORE ABOUT JESUS IS NOT ALWAYS THE SAME AS BECOMING MORE LIKE JESUS.
That sentence should trouble us.
Especially those of us who love theology.
Because theological knowledge is a gift.
Studying the Bible deeply is good.
Learning biblical languages can be valuable.
Understanding church history can protect us from repeating old errors.
Defending sound doctrine is necessary.
But knowledge can become dangerous when it feeds pride instead of worship.
Paul wrote:
“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” (1 Corinthians 8:1, ESV)
The Greek expression ἡ γνῶσις φυσιοῖ — hē gnōsis physioi conveys the idea that knowledge can inflate or puff someone up.
Paul was not condemning knowledge itself.
He was confronting knowledge used without love.
And there is a painful irony here.
A person can accurately explain the doctrine of justification while treating other believers with a spirit that contradicts the humility that justification should produce.
Someone can correctly defend the sovereignty of God while behaving as though God's throne needs their personal arrogance to remain secure.
Someone can preach the sufficiency of Christ while acting as though Christ's finished work must be supplemented by agreement with every one of their secondary interpretations.
But the Gospel leaves no room for boasting.
If salvation is grace, then nobody gets to stand before God and say:
“I deserved to be here because I understood everything.”
No.
The redeemed will praise the Lamb who was slain.
Not the brilliance of their own theological systems.
AND YET, GRACE IS NEVER PERMISSION TO REMAIN CARELESS ABOUT TRUTH.
Perhaps someone reading this has been wounded by harsh, argumentative Christians.
Maybe you were publicly embarrassed because you asked a sincere question.
Maybe somebody questioned your salvation because you did not share their interpretation of a disputed passage.
Maybe you were made to feel that you could never belong to Jesus unless you understood every theological term.
If that happened, I want you to hear something clearly.
You do not need to pretend you know what you do not know.
You are allowed to ask questions.
You are allowed to study.
You are allowed to admit that a passage is difficult.
And you are allowed to change your mind when Scripture corrects you.
But do not let the cruelty of an argumentative believer convince you that doctrine itself is the enemy.
Truth is not your enemy.
Jesus prayed:
“Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.” (John 17:17, ESV)
The answer to spiritual arrogance is not biblical ignorance.
The answer is humble submission to God's Word.
A teachable heart does not say, “Doctrine doesn't matter.”
It says, “Lord, Your truth matters so much that I am willing to be corrected.”
There is a profound difference between being mistaken and being unteachable.
A sincere believer may misunderstand a secondary doctrine while genuinely desiring to obey Christ.
Another person may cling to error because admitting the truth would threaten their reputation, influence, or pride.
God sees what we cannot fully see.
And that is why theological humility must never become theological indifference.
We should hold our convictions seriously.
But we should hold ourselves humbly.
PETER WAS TRULY CHRIST'S DISCIPLE—AND HE STILL NEEDED TO BE CORRECTED.
Think about Peter.
He confessed Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16).
Yet soon afterward, he resisted Jesus' announcement of His coming suffering and death.
Jesus rebuked him sharply (Matthew 16:21–23).
Later, Peter denied knowing Jesus three times.
And after the resurrection, Christ graciously restored him (John 21:15–19).
Still later, Paul publicly confronted Peter because his conduct toward Gentile believers was not consistent with the truth of the Gospel (Galatians 2:11–14).
Peter was not a model of perfect understanding or flawless behavior.
He was a man transformed by a faithful Savior who corrected him, restored him, and continued to use him.
Now, Peter's mistakes were not harmless.
His conduct in Galatians threatened the practical expression of Gospel truth.
Paul confronted him because the Gospel mattered.
But the account also shows that even a genuine apostle could act inconsistently with what he knew.
Correction was necessary.
Grace was still real.
That is not an excuse for sin.
It is a testimony to the patience of Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear it.
You may be wrong about something today.
You may discover next year that a position you defended with great confidence was mistaken.
You may need to repent of the way you treated people who disagreed with you.
You may need to revisit passages you thought you had completely understood.
But discovering your own limitations does not mean Jesus has abandoned you.
It may be part of how He is teaching you to depend more deeply on Him.
THERE IS A DIFFERENCE BETWEEN GROWING IN TRUTH AND MAKING YOUR OWN UNDERSTANDING THE SAVIOR.
Paul described Christian maturity as something believers grow toward.
In Philippians 3:12, he openly acknowledged that he had not already obtained perfection.
And in Philippians 3:15–16, he spoke of believers continuing forward, trusting God to clarify what they did not yet understand.
That is remarkable.
The apostle who wrote so much of the New Testament recognized that spiritual growth was not complete.
Now consider the implications.
If Christian maturity involves growth, then immaturity cannot automatically mean the absence of salvation.
If believers are commanded to grow in the grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ (2 Peter 3:18), then growth necessarily involves moving from less understanding toward greater understanding.
A new Christian may not know the meaning of eschatology.
A struggling believer may not understand the distinctions between various interpretations of Revelation.
A faithful elderly Christian may never have studied biblical Greek.
A poor believer with limited access to theological education may know little about historic doctrinal controversies.
Does that mean Christ cannot save them?
No.
The Gospel was never reserved for the intellectually privileged.
The same Jesus who welcomes scholars also welcomes children.
The same grace that reaches trained theologians reaches repentant sinners who can barely find words to pray.
The decisive issue is not whether someone can explain every dimension of Christian theology.
It is whether they truly belong to Jesus Christ.
And belonging to Christ is not a license to ignore His teaching.
It is the beginning of a life in which we learn to follow Him.
BUT WHAT ABOUT THE CHRISTIAN WHO IS SINCERELY WRONG?
This is where we need to be especially careful.
Sincerity alone does not save.
People can sincerely believe things that are false.
The Bible never teaches that every sincere religious belief leads to eternal life.
Jesus said:
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” (John 14:6, ESV)
Salvation is found in Christ.
Not sincerity detached from Christ.
Not moral effort.
Not religious identity.
Not theological achievement.
Christ.
But a Christian can sincerely trust the true Christ while misunderstanding some of His teachings.
That is different from rejecting who Christ is or denying the Gospel that saves.
We must also distinguish between ignorance, confusion, honest disagreement, deliberate distortion, and persistent rebellion against clearly understood truth.
These are not spiritually identical.
Only God perfectly knows the heart.
We can evaluate a person's confession, teaching, and conduct according to Scripture.
We can identify false doctrine.
We can warn against dangerous teaching.
Churches can establish doctrinal boundaries for membership, leadership, and ministry.
But we should be extremely cautious about claiming to know with certainty the eternal state of every person who disagrees with us on a disputed secondary issue.
Jesus did not appoint us as omniscient judges of the human soul.
He commanded us to make disciples.
To teach His Word.
To love one another.
To proclaim repentance and forgiveness in His name.
And to remain faithful until He comes.
THE MOST DANGEROUS QUESTION MAY NOT BE, “WHAT IF MY BROTHER IS WRONG?”
It may be:
“What if I am the one who needs correction?”
That question takes courage.
Because pride loves certainty more than truth.
Pride wants to win.
Humility wants to understand.
Pride asks, “How can I prove this person wrong?”
Humility asks, “Lord, what does Your Word actually say?”
Pride treats correction as humiliation.
Humility receives correction as an opportunity to grow.
And the truly frightening thing about pride is that it can hide behind correct theology.
You can defend a true doctrine with a sinful spirit.
You can win an argument and wound a brother.
You can be right about a passage while being terribly wrong about how you treat the person standing in front of you.
James 3:17 describes wisdom from above as pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, and sincere.
That is not weak Christianity.
That is biblical maturity.
Truth without love can become a weapon of self-exaltation.
Love without truth can become sentimental compromise.
But truth and love together reflect the character of Jesus Christ.
John 1:14 describes Him as full of grace and truth.
Not half grace and half truth.
Not grace at the expense of truth.
Not truth stripped of grace.
Full of both.
And every Christian who claims to follow Him should desire the same.
SOMEONE YOU DISAGREE WITH MAY BE YOUR BROTHER OR SISTER IN ETERNITY.
Think about that for a moment.
The believer whose interpretation frustrates you.
The Christian whose denominational background is different from yours.
The person who worships with a style you find unfamiliar.
The brother who has not reached your conclusion about a disputed theological issue.
If that person truly belongs to Jesus Christ, you may spend eternity worshiping the same Savior together.
Not because truth did not matter.
Not because all doctrinal disagreements were equally harmless.
But because both of you were redeemed by the same blood.
Revelation 7:9 portrays a multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language standing before the throne and before the Lamb.
The redeemed are united in worship.
Their salvation is centered on God and the Lamb.
And when that day comes, none of us will boast about the theological arguments we won.
We will worship the Christ who saved us.
Perhaps we will finally understand just how much we misunderstood.
Scripture does not give us a detailed account of every correction that may occur in eternity, so we should not invent one.
But it does promise that our present knowledge is partial.
Paul writes:
Our understanding is real.
But it is not exhaustive.
Our knowledge can be true.
But it is not infinite.
We know enough through God's revelation to trust Christ, obey His commands, and proclaim His Gospel.
Yet we still await the fullness of what God will reveal.
That should not make us uncertain about Jesus.
It should make us humble about ourselves.
SO CAN A CHRISTIAN BE SAVED WHILE HOLDING INCORRECT BELIEFS ABOUT SECONDARY DOCTRINES?
Yes.
A genuine Christian can be saved while holding mistaken beliefs about secondary doctrines.
Because salvation is grounded in the grace of God through faith in Jesus Christ, not in perfect mastery of every theological question.
But that answer comes with important biblical qualifications.
The Gospel itself cannot be treated as optional.
Not every disputed doctrine is automatically secondary.
Not every claim of faith is genuine.
Not every error is harmless.
And grace never removes our responsibility to seek truth, receive correction, repent of sin, and grow in obedience.
A Christian who is mistaken should be taught patiently.
A Christian who is confused should be helped compassionately.
A Christian who is proud should be corrected lovingly.
A Christian who distorts the Gospel should be warned seriously.
And every Christian, regardless of knowledge or maturity, should be pointed continually back to Jesus Christ.
Because Christianity is not merely about having the correct answers.
It is about being reconciled to the living God through His Son.
And the more deeply we understand that Gospel, the less room we should have for spiritual arrogance.
THIS IS WHERE SCANDAL MEETS GRACE.
The scandal is that sinners who do not deserve eternal life can be welcomed into God's family.
The scandal is that people with broken histories, incomplete understanding, embarrassing failures, and painful regrets can receive forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
The scandal is that the proud religious expert and the trembling new believer must enter through the same door.
Grace.
Not earned.
Not purchased.
Not achieved through intellectual superiority.
Received through faith in the crucified and risen Savior.
But grace does not leave us unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace corrects.
Grace transforms.
And the Jesus who saves us also calls us to follow Him.
Maybe your scandal was not a public moral failure.
Maybe it was pride.
Maybe you used theology to feel superior.
Maybe you mocked Christians who had not studied as much as you.
Maybe you confused your denomination's distinctives with the boundaries of salvation itself.
Or maybe your scandal was fear.
You spent years wondering whether Jesus would reject you because you could not understand every difficult passage.
You quietly worried that one mistaken interpretation might erase your hope of eternal life.
You loved Christ.
You wanted to obey Him.
But you were terrified that your imperfect understanding made you unacceptable to God.
If that is you, hear the invitation of Jesus.
“Whoever comes to me I will never cast out.” (John 6:37, ESV)
Do not turn that promise into permission to ignore Scripture.
Let it become the reason you run toward Him.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come willing to learn.
Come ready to surrender what Scripture exposes.
And trust the Savior who is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25).
You do not need to pretend that you have all the answers.
You need the One who is the Truth.
AND IF YOU HAVE NEVER TRULY SURRENDERED YOUR LIFE TO CHRIST, THIS IS MORE THAN A THEOLOGICAL DISCUSSION.
You can spend your entire life debating salvation without ever personally trusting the Savior.
You can know Christian vocabulary without knowing Christ.
You can memorize doctrines while refusing to repent.
You can defend the Bible publicly while resisting its authority privately.
And you can be surrounded by religious activity while remaining spiritually far from God.
That is why the central question is not merely whether you hold an incorrect secondary doctrine.
The deeper question is whether you have truly placed your faith in Jesus Christ.
Have you acknowledged your sin before God?
Have you trusted in Christ's death and resurrection as your only hope of salvation?
Are you willing to turn from sin and follow Him as Lord?
Not perfectly.
Not without struggle.
But sincerely.
Because saving faith is not merely agreeing that certain religious statements are true.
It is trusting in the living Christ whom those truths reveal.
Romans 10:9 connects confessing Jesus as Lord and believing that God raised Him from the dead with salvation.
And Romans 10:13 declares:
“For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.” (ESV)
That invitation remains open.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Jesus is sufficient.
Not because truth is optional.
But because the Truth Himself came to rescue sinners.
If you need to return to Him, you can pray in your own words.

“Lord Jesus, I confess that I am a sinner who needs Your mercy. Forgive my pride, my unbelief, and my rebellion. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Teach me to trust Your Word above my opinions, to love others without compromising truth, and to follow You with a humble and obedient heart. I cannot save myself. My hope is in You alone. Amen.”
A prayer is not a magical formula.
Christ saves, not the mere repetition of words.
But if those words express the sincere cry of your heart, do not delay in turning to Him.
And do not try to walk alone.
Find a faithful, Bible-teaching local church where you can be discipled, baptized if you have not been, encouraged, corrected, and equipped to grow in Christ.
BEFORE YOU LEAVE, THERE IS SOMETHING I WANT TO ASK YOU.
Have you ever been made to feel that you were not a real Christian because you disagreed with someone about a secondary doctrine?
Or have you ever realized that you were the person who treated another believer harshly because of a theological disagreement?
Be honest.
Not to win another argument.
Not to embarrass anyone.
But because spiritual healing often begins when we stop pretending we have nothing left to learn.
If this message exposed pride in your heart, you can comment, “Lord, teach me humility.”
If you have been wounded by harsh religious judgment and are learning to trust Jesus again, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
You may need to return to it the next time a theological argument begins to harden your heart.
You may need its reminder when somebody challenges a conviction you have held for years.
Or when you discover that you were wrong.
Because spiritual maturity is not demonstrated only by how strongly we defend what we believe.
Sometimes it is demonstrated by how humbly we respond when God's Word corrects us.
AND MAYBE SOMEONE YOU LOVE NEEDS TO READ THIS TODAY.
There may be a friend on your Facebook feed who has quietly walked away from Christian fellowship after being wounded by needless condemnation.
There may be a young believer who is afraid to ask questions.
There may be a family member who has mistaken religious arguments for the heart of Christianity.
There may even be someone who has never understood that salvation is a gift of grace through Jesus Christ.
Not merely to increase its reach.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you grow in your faith, I want to invite you into something deeper.
HELP US KEEP BRINGING THE GOSPEL TO PEOPLE WHO NEED IT.
Every article written, every biblical resource shared, and every message of encouragement is part of a larger mission: to point people away from themselves and toward Jesus Christ.
We want those resources to continue reaching people who may never be able to purchase a Christian book, attend a conference, or afford a discipleship program.
That work requires time, resources, and faithful support.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful—not forced by guilt or spiritual pressure (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And your responsibility to support your local church and care for those entrusted to you should never be displaced by pressure from an online ministry.
Those products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
You can pray for the ministry.
You can use the free resources and continue growing in God's Word.
The Gospel is not for sale.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
What matters is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully, His Word is handled truthfully, and people are invited to know and follow Him.
BECAUSE ONE DAY, EVERY ARGUMENT WILL END.
The comment sections will go silent.
The debates will be over.
The theological disagreements that consumed so much of our time will finally be placed beneath the perfect knowledge and righteous judgment of God.
And every person will stand before the Lord.
On that day, the only Savior who can redeem us will not be our theological intelligence.
It will be Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The Lamb of God.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who conquered the grave.
The One who calls His people to truth, holiness, humility, and love.
So study deeply.
Defend the Gospel faithfully.
Reject false teaching.
Receive correction.
Love the brethren.
Never confuse humility with compromise.
Never confuse conviction with cruelty.
And never forget that the same grace you desperately need is the grace you should never be ashamed to celebrate when Christ extends it to another repentant sinner.
Because the question is not whether you will ever discover that you were wrong about something.
You almost certainly will.
The question is whether you will allow God's Word to correct you—and whether your confidence rests in your own understanding or in the finished work of Jesus Christ.

You may reach heaven having misunderstood some things about God, but you will never reach heaven apart from the mercy of the God who understood everything about you—and loved you enough to send His Son to save you.
